segments.text: Every living thing can repair itself a little. Yet almost everything ages and dies. If evolution can build an eye, why can't it build a body that lasts forever?
The answer begins with a simple fact about selection: it is strongest when you are young, and it fades as you grow older.
Most individuals die from accidents, predators, or disease before they reach old age. A mutation that harms you at eighty is almost invisible to selection, because almost nobody gets there.
That fading force has two consequences. The first is mutation accumulation: harmful mutations that act late in life slip in, and selection is too weak to remove them.
The second consequence is antagonistic pleiotropy. A gene that helps you reproduce early can spread through the population, even if the same gene makes you decline later in life.
To see this, we built a small world. Each blob carries a genome, ages, and reproduces. Mutations appear at random ages, and death comes from both the environment and the genome.
In a dangerous world, most blobs die young. Selection pushes reproduction earlier, and lifespan stays short.
Remove some of that danger, and more blobs survive to old age. Selection can now see later ages, and a longer lifespan evolves.
But aging never disappears. In both worlds, the risk of death rises with age, because late-acting mutations keep accumulating.
The mortality curve shifts when the environment changes, but its shape stays the same. The force of selection always fades with age.
Real biology is messier. Repair, trade-offs, and environment all interact. But the core logic is simple.
Aging is not the body failing. It is the shadow cast by selection, fading as we grow older.
